items.stem: Which of the following best describes "research question"?
options: Unpredictable variation in readings that makes repeats differ; reduced by repeating and averaging
A table with the independent variable in the first column and the dependent variable (with repeats and mean) in the next columns, with units in the headings
A version of the experiment without the factor being tested, used for comparison
The focused question an investigation sets out to answer, naming the independent and dependent variables
items.answer: The focused question an investigation sets out to answer, naming the independent and dependent variables
items.markingKey: D. "research question" is the focused question an investigation sets out to answer, naming the independent and dependent variables.

items.stem: "A hypothesis is just a guess." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A hypothesis is an educated prediction based on scientific knowledge and includes a reason; it is testable.
items.markingKey: A hypothesis is an educated prediction based on scientific knowledge and includes a reason; it is testable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a research question should name both the independent and dependent variables.
items.answer: It makes clear exactly what will be changed and what will be measured, so the investigation is focused and others can repeat it. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It makes clear exactly what will be changed and what will be measured, so the investigation is focused and others can repeat it. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Yusuf plans to investigate how the temperature of water affects the time taken for a sugar cube to dissolve. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: volume of water (100 cm³); type and size of sugar cube; stirring (none or the same rate); type of container
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: volume of water (100 cm³) – more water would dissolve the sugar faster; type and size of sugar cube – smaller pieces dissolve faster; stirring (none or the same rate) – stirring speeds dissolving; type of container – affects heat loss. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Using Barry Marshall and stomach ulcers (1984) as an example, explain testing a hypothesis against accepted ideas.
items.answer: Marshall hypothesised that bacteria (Helicobacter pylori), not stress, caused ulcers, and drank a culture to test it; he developed gastritis, which antibiotics cured. Evidence from a test supported a new hypothesis and changed medical treatment; he shared the 2005 Nobel Prize.
items.markingKey: Context (Marshall hypothesised that bacteria (Helicobacter pylori), not stress, caused ulcers, and drank a culture to test it; he developed gastritis, which antibiotics cured.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Evidence from a test supported a new hypothesis and changed medical treatment; he shared the 2005 Nobel Prize. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to testing a hypothesis against accepted ideas.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Citizen science projects, where members of the public collect data, produce useful science."
items.answer: With good design, training and checking, citizen science produces valuable data that professionals alone could not collect.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: huge amounts of data over wide areas (e.g. bird counts, Galaxy Zoo); engages people with science. Arguments against: data quality may vary without training; needs careful checking by scientists. Supported judgement: With good design, training and checking, citizen science produces valuable data that professionals alone could not collect.

items.stem: Which statement is a hypothesis rather than an observation?
options: The plant was watered on Monday.
If the light is brighter, then the plant will grow taller, because it can photosynthesise faster.
items.answer: If the light is brighter, then the plant will grow taller, because it can photosynthesise faster.
items.markingKey: C. A hypothesis is a testable prediction with a reason.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a hypothesis and an observation.
items.answer: An observation is something noticed or measured; a hypothesis is a testable prediction with a scientific reason that explains an observation.
items.markingKey: An observation is something noticed or measured; a hypothesis is a testable prediction with a scientific reason that explains an observation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Priya observes that a ball bounces higher on the playground than on the grass. Write a testable research question and a hypothesis, with a scientific reason, that could be investigated.
items.answer: Research question: How does the surface the ball is dropped on affect the bounce height? Hypothesis: changing the surface the ball is dropped on will change the bounce height, because a soft surface absorbs more of the ball’s energy.
items.markingKey: 1 research question naming the IV (surface the ball is dropped on) and a measurable DV (bounce height); 1 testable prediction ("if … then …"); 1 scientific reason: a soft surface absorbs more of the ball’s energy.

items.stem: Arjun plans an investigation into how the temperature of water affects the time taken for a sugar cube to dissolve. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (temperature of the water (°C)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the height of a ramp affects the speed of a toy car, what is the dependent variable?
items.answer: The speed of the car
items.markingKey: The speed of the car. It is what is measured.

items.stem: A student claims: "The dependent variable is the one you control." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: You change the independent variable; you measure the dependent variable; control variables are kept the same.
items.markingKey: You change the independent variable; you measure the dependent variable; control variables are kept the same. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why changing two variables at once makes an investigation invalid.
items.answer: If two variables are changed together, you cannot tell which one caused the change in the dependent variable. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If two variables are changed together, you cannot tell which one caused the change in the dependent variable. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Mei is investigating how the surface area of a tablet affects how quickly it fizzes away in water. State the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables.
items.answer: IV: surface area of the tablet (whole, halves, quarters, powder); DV: time to stop fizzing; controls: volume and temperature of water, brand of tablet
items.markingKey: 1 IV surface area of the tablet (whole, halves, quarters, powder); 1 DV time to stop fizzing; 1-2 any two valid controls from: volume and temperature of water, brand of tablet.

items.stem: Elena is investigating how the length of a pendulum affects the time for one complete swing. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: length of the pendulum string (cm)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: length of the pendulum string (cm) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Sofia measured the time for 10 swings of a pendulum of different lengths and calculated the period of one swing.

Length / cm | Period / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
20 | 0.83 | 0.84 | 0.83
40 | 1.24 | 1.21 | 1.16
60 | 1.48 | 1.52 | 1.43
80 | 1.70 | 1.75 | 1.64
100 | 1.90 | 1.85 | 1.96

Calculate the mean period when the length was 80 cm.
items.markingKey: M1 (1.70 + 1.75 + 1.64) ÷ 3; A1 1.70 s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Clinical drug trials should always include a control group given a placebo."
items.answer: Control groups are essential, but ethics decide whether they receive a placebo or the current best treatment.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows whether improvement is due to the drug or to expectation (placebo effect); makes the comparison fair. Arguments against: withholding treatment from very ill patients is unethical when an effective treatment exists – then the new drug is compared with the existing one. Supported judgement: Control groups are essential, but ethics decide whether they receive a placebo or the current best treatment.

items.stem: Amara plans an investigation into how the length of a pendulum affects the time for one complete swing. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (length of the pendulum string (cm)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Briefly explain why changing two variables at once makes an investigation invalid.
items.answer: If two variables are changed together, you cannot tell which one caused the change in the dependent variable.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If two variables are changed together, you cannot tell which one caused the change in the dependent variable. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the dependent variable and the independent variable.
items.answer: The independent variable is what you change on purpose; the dependent variable is what you measure in response.
items.markingKey: The independent variable is what you change on purpose; the dependent variable is what you measure in response. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Nia writes: "A fair test means doing the experiment only once so nothing changes." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A fair test changes only the independent variable; repeating trials improves reliability.
items.markingKey: A fair test changes only the independent variable; repeating trials improves reliability. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mei is investigating how the concentration of salt water affects the mass change of potato chips. State the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables.
items.answer: IV: salt concentration; DV: change in mass of the chips; controls: size of chips, time in solution, volume of solution, temperature
items.markingKey: 1 IV salt concentration; 1 DV change in mass of the chips; 1-2 any two valid controls from: size of chips, time in solution, volume of solution, temperature.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An internationally recognised (GHS) pictogram warning of a danger, e.g. flammable, corrosive, toxic"?
items.answer: hazard symbol
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of hazard symbol.

items.stem: Distinguish between precision and accuracy.
items.answer: Accurate measurements are close to the true value; precise measurements are close to each other (small spread) but could all be wrong.
items.markingKey: Accurate measurements are close to the true value; precise measurements are close to each other (small spread) but could all be wrong. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why scientists around the world use SI units.
items.answer: A common system means results can be compared and repeated anywhere, avoiding errors from converting between units (e.g. the 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter loss).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A common system means results can be compared and repeated anywhere, avoiding errors from converting between units (e.g. the 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter loss). (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In an investigation into which type of measuring apparatus (beaker, measuring cylinder, burette) gives the most accurate measurement of 25 cm³ of water, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: temperature of the water.
items.answer: density changes slightly with temperature
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (temperature of the water) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: density changes slightly with temperature. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: Briefly describe the loss of NASA’s Mars Climate Orbiter (1999) and explain what it reveals about the importance of SI units.
items.answer: One team used imperial units (pound-force seconds) and another used SI units (newton seconds); the spacecraft entered the atmosphere too low and was destroyed. Mixing unit systems caused a calculation error worth US$125 million – using one agreed system avoids this.
items.markingKey: Context (One team used imperial units (pound-force seconds) and another used SI units (newton seconds); the spacecraft entered the atmosphere too low and was destroyed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Mixing unit systems caused a calculation error worth US$125 million – using one agreed system avoids this. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of SI units.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for heating copper(II) sulfate solution in an evaporating basin over a Bunsen burner. Include three hazards, the risk from each and a precaution for each.
items.answer: Hot apparatus/liquid – burns or scalds – use tongs, heat-proof mat, let cool; spitting solution – eye injury – wear eye protection, stop heating when crystals start to form; copper(II) sulfate is harmful/irritant – skin and eye irritation, harmful if swallowed – gloves, wash hands; Bunsen flame – hair or clothing catching fire – tie hair back, use safety flame when not heating.
items.markingKey: Hot apparatus/liquid – burns or scalds – use tongs, heat-proof mat, let cool; spitting solution – eye injury – wear eye protection, stop heating when crystals start to form; copper(II) sulfate is harmful/irritant – skin and eye irritation, harmful if swallowed – gloves, wash hands; Bunsen flame – hair or clothing catching fire – tie hair back, use safety flame when not heating.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "risk assessment"?
options: A relationship where doubling one variable doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin
A prediction of the outcome of an investigation, with a scientific reason, that can be tested
Identifying hazards in an investigation, how likely and serious harm is, and the precautions to reduce the risk
A table with the independent variable in the first column and the dependent variable (with repeats and mean) in the next columns, with units in the headings
items.answer: Identifying hazards in an investigation, how likely and serious harm is, and the precautions to reduce the risk
items.markingKey: C. "risk assessment" is identifying hazards in an investigation, how likely and serious harm is, and the precautions to reduce the risk.

items.stem: "A beaker is the best apparatus for measuring 37 cm³ of water." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Beakers have rough scales; a 50 cm³ measuring cylinder (or burette) gives a much more accurate volume.
items.markingKey: Beakers have rough scales; a 50 cm³ measuring cylinder (or burette) gives a much more accurate volume. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Noah measured the volume of gas collected in four repeats: 28.7, 21.8, 22.7, 22.5 cm³. Calculate the mean volume and the range of the results.
items.answer: mean 23.93 cm³; range 6.9 cm³

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into which type of measuring apparatus (beaker, measuring cylinder, burette) gives the most accurate measurement of 25 cm³ of water. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): mop up spills to avoid slipping; handle glass carefully. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. mop up spills to avoid slipping; handle glass carefully); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Where should the units be written in a results table?
items.answer: In the column headings
items.markingKey: In the column headings. e.g. "Time / s".

items.stem: Distinguish between a positive correlation and a negative correlation.
items.answer: In a positive correlation the dependent variable increases as the independent variable increases; in a negative correlation it decreases.
items.markingKey: In a positive correlation the dependent variable increases as the independent variable increases; in a negative correlation it decreases. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the mean of repeated readings is used instead of a single reading.
items.answer: Random errors make individual readings vary; averaging several readings reduces the effect of random error and gives a more reliable value.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Random errors make individual readings vary; averaging several readings reduces the effect of random error and gives a more reliable value. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Freya hung masses on a spring and measured its extension, repeating each reading three times.

Mass / g | Extension / cm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
100 | 1.7 | 1.7 | 1.8
200 | 3.5 | 3.4 | 3.3
300 | 4.9 | 5.0 | 5.1
400 | 7.1 | 7.0 | 6.8
500 | 8.5 | 8.3 | 8.5

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: Extension increases in direct proportion to the mass added – doubling the mass doubles the extension. Each 100 g adds about 1 N of force; the spring obeys Hooke’s law (extension ∝ force) below its elastic limit.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: Extension increases in direct proportion to the mass added – doubling the mass doubles the extension.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Each 100 g adds about 1 N of force; the spring obeys Hooke’s law (extension ∝ force) below its elastic limit.

items.stem: Ana wants to find out how the mass hung on a spring affects the extension of the spring. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does mass hung on the spring affect extension?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (mass hung on the spring (100 g to 600 g in 100 g steps)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (extension – new length minus original length, measured with a metre rule to the nearest mm) in a question form.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Graphs in news reports always represent data honestly."
items.answer: Graphs can mislead; readers should check axes, scales and sources before drawing conclusions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: graphs make data easy to understand quickly. Arguments against: axes that do not start at zero can exaggerate changes; selecting time periods can hide trends; correlation may be presented as causation. Supported judgement: Graphs can mislead; readers should check axes, scales and sources before drawing conclusions.

items.stem: Define the term "directly proportional".
items.answer: A relationship where doubling one variable doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a relationship where doubling one variable doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "A line of best fit must go through every point, joining them dot to dot." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A line of best fit is a single smooth line or curve with points scattered evenly either side; it does not join dot to dot.
items.markingKey: A line of best fit is a single smooth line or curve with points scattered evenly either side; it does not join dot to dot. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A straight-line graph of extension (cm, y-axis) against load (N, x-axis) passes through (2 N, 4 cm) and (8 N, 16 cm). Calculate the gradient and give its units.
items.answer: 2 cm/N
items.markingKey: M1 gradient = change in y ÷ change in x = (16 − 4) ÷ (8 − 2); A1 2 cm/N.

items.stem: A student’s table of results has no units, the repeats are not averaged and the independent variable is in the last column. Describe four improvements to the table and explain how each makes the data easier to use.
items.answer: Put the IV in the first column (it is what was chosen); add units to headings, e.g. "Temperature / °C" (values have meaning); add a mean column and calculate means (reduces effect of random errors); use a consistent number of decimal places matching the instrument (shows precision); highlight/exclude anomalies.
items.markingKey: Put the IV in the first column (it is what was chosen); add units to headings, e.g. "Temperature / °C" (values have meaning); add a mean column and calculate means (reduces effect of random errors); use a consistent number of decimal places matching the instrument (shows precision); highlight/exclude anomalies.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "How consistent results are when an investigation is repeated"?
items.answer: reliability
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of reliability.

items.stem: Explain why scientists ask other scientists to repeat their experiments.
items.answer: If independent scientists get the same results with different equipment, the results are reproducible and more likely to be correct.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If independent scientists get the same results with different equipment, the results are reproducible and more likely to be correct. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A class measured the boiling point of water (°C) as 97.5. The accepted value is 100.0. Calculate the percentage difference.
A student claims: "Human error means I made a mistake, so it should be in every evaluation." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Evaluations should name the specific source of error (e.g. reaction time when using a stopwatch) and suggest a specific improvement.
items.markingKey: Evaluations should name the specific source of error (e.g. reaction time when using a stopwatch) and suggest a specific improvement. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the method of timing (hand-held stopwatch or light gates) affects the reliability of measuring the time for a ball to roll down a 1.0 m ramp. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): catch the ball at the end of the ramp; keep the floor clear. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. catch the ball at the end of the ramp; keep the floor clear); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Explain why repeating readings does not remove a systematic error.
items.answer: A systematic error shifts every reading by the same amount, so the repeats agree with each other but are all wrong; the cause (e.g. zero error) must be corrected.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A systematic error shifts every reading by the same amount, so the repeats agree with each other but are all wrong; the cause (e.g. zero error) must be corrected. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Tariq and three classmates each timed a ball rolling down the same ramp with stopwatches, three times each, while the ramp height was changed.

Ramp height / cm | Time / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 2.84 | 2.79 | 2.97
20 | 2.06 | 2.00 | 2.00
30 | 1.71 | 1.73 | 1.70
40 | 1.47 | 1.47 | 1.49
50 | 1.27 | 1.31 | 1.26

Calculate the percentage change in the mean time between 10 cm and 50 cm.
items.markingKey: M1 means 2.87 and 1.28; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 -55.3% (decrease).

items.stem: A student measured how the height a ball is dropped from affects its bounce height, using a metre rule held by hand and judging the top of each bounce by eye, with one drop per height. Evaluate the method, identifying two sources of error and suggesting a specific improvement for each.
items.answer: Judging the bounce top by eye is difficult (random error, parallax) – film the bounce in slow motion against a fixed scale; one drop per height gives unreliable data – repeat 3-5 times and calculate means, identifying anomalies; ruler held by hand may move – clamp it vertically. The conclusion would then be more reliable and valid.
items.markingKey: Judging the bounce top by eye is difficult (random error, parallax) – film the bounce in slow motion against a fixed scale; one drop per height gives unreliable data – repeat 3-5 times and calculate means, identifying anomalies; ruler held by hand may move – clamp it vertically. The conclusion would then be more reliable and valid.

items.stem: Define the term "control variable".
items.answer: A variable that is kept the same so that it does not affect the results
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a variable that is kept the same so that it does not affect the results. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "testable question".
items.answer: A question that can be answered by changing one variable and measuring the effect on another
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a question that can be answered by changing one variable and measuring the effect on another. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which apparatus would a student use to separate a solid from a liquid?
items.answer: Filter funnel and filter paper
items.markingKey: B. Filter funnel and filter paper is designed for this measurement.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "Correlation always means one variable causes the other." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A correlation shows a link; a third factor may cause both (e.g. ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in hot weather).
items.markingKey: A correlation shows a link; a third factor may cause both (e.g. ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in hot weather). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between systematic error and random error.
items.answer: Random errors make readings scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift all readings the same way and need the cause correcting.
items.markingKey: Random errors make readings scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift all readings the same way and need the cause correcting. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a control experiment and a control variable.
items.answer: A control variable is a factor kept the same in every trial; a control experiment is a separate set-up without the factor being tested, used for comparison.
items.markingKey: A control variable is a factor kept the same in every trial; a control experiment is a separate set-up without the factor being tested, used for comparison. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why a research question should name both the independent and dependent variables.
items.answer: It makes clear exactly what will be changed and what will be measured, so the investigation is focused and others can repeat it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It makes clear exactly what will be changed and what will be measured, so the investigation is focused and others can repeat it. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why you should read a measuring cylinder at eye level.
items.answer: Looking from above or below causes parallax error, making the reading seem too high or too low.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Looking from above or below causes parallax error, making the reading seem too high or too low. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a line graph and a bar chart.
items.answer: A bar chart is used when the independent variable is categoric (types); a line graph is used when both variables are continuous numbers.
items.markingKey: A bar chart is used when the independent variable is categoric (types); a line graph is used when both variables are continuous numbers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the 1989 “cold fusion” claim by Fleischmann and Pons as an example, explain reproducibility and reliability.
items.answer: They announced nuclear fusion at room temperature in a simple cell; laboratories around the world could not reproduce the results. Because independent repeats failed, the scientific community rejected the claim – results must be reproducible to be accepted.
items.markingKey: Context (They announced nuclear fusion at room temperature in a simple cell; laboratories around the world could not reproduce the results.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Because independent repeats failed, the scientific community rejected the claim – results must be reproducible to be accepted. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reproducibility and reliability.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the length of a pendulum affects the time for one complete swing, state the dependent variable and describe how Freya should measure it.
items.answer: time period – time for 10 swings measured with a stopwatch, divided by 10
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: time period – time for 10 swings measured with a stopwatch, divided by 10.

items.stem:
Tariq timed how long a sugar cube took to dissolve in 100 cm³ of water at different temperatures, without stirring.

Temperature / °C | Time to dissolve / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
20 | 304 | 311 | 294
30 | 225 | 229 | 224
40 | 240 | 175 | 186
50 | 146 | 150 | 154
60 | 131 | 134 | 133

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean time to dissolve at 40 °C, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 240 s (trial 1 at 40 °C); mean = 180.5 s
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (240) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 180.5 s.

items.stem:
Ingrid measured the temperature of a beaker of water heated on a hot plate every 2 minutes, repeating the experiment three times.

Time / min | Temperature / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 32.3 | 31.8 | 32.3
4 | 59.3 | 42.4 | 43.6
6 | 53.3 | 55.2 | 54.1
8 | 69.3 | 67.2 | 68.1
10 | 80.0 | 76.1 | 81.3

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean temperature at 4 min, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 59.3 °C (trial 1 at 4 min); mean = 43.00 °C
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (59.3) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 43.00 °C.

items.stem:
Mateo hung masses on a spring and measured its extension, repeating each reading three times.

Mass / g | Extension / cm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
100 | 1.9 | 2.0 | 2.0
200 | 4.0 | 4.0 | 3.9
300 | 5.8 | 6.0 | 5.8
400 | 7.9 | 8.0 | 8.1
500 | 10.0 | 9.6 | 9.6

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: Extension increases in direct proportion to the mass added – doubling the mass doubles the extension. Each 100 g adds about 1 N of force; the spring obeys Hooke’s law (extension ∝ force) below its elastic limit.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: Extension increases in direct proportion to the mass added – doubling the mass doubles the extension.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Each 100 g adds about 1 N of force; the spring obeys Hooke’s law (extension ∝ force) below its elastic limit.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the method of timing (hand-held stopwatch or light gates) affects the reliability of measuring the time for a ball to roll down a 1.0 m ramp, explain why the same ball released from rest must be used in every trial.
items.answer: pushing changes the time
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (the same ball released from rest) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: pushing changes the time. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem:
Zara measured the time for 10 swings of a pendulum of different lengths and calculated the period of one swing.

Length / cm | Period / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
20 | 0.85 | 0.86 | 0.89
40 | 1.24 | 1.17 | 1.18
60 | 1.43 | 1.43 | 1.51
80 | 1.73 | 1.78 | 1.67
100 | 1.99 | 1.92 | 1.95

State the length at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 80 cm; range = 0.11 s; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 80 cm; 1 range = max − min = 1.78 − 1.67 = 0.11 s; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: A student notices that bread goes mouldy faster in the kitchen than in the fridge. Write a testable research question, a hypothesis with a scientific reason, and state the independent and dependent variables for an investigation.
items.answer: Question: How does temperature affect the time taken for mould to appear on bread? Hypothesis: if temperature is higher (up to about 30 °C), mould appears sooner, because fungal enzymes work faster and spores grow more quickly. IV: temperature; DV: days until mould is first visible (or area covered after 5 days).
items.markingKey: Question: How does temperature affect the time taken for mould to appear on bread? Hypothesis: if temperature is higher (up to about 30 °C), mould appears sooner, because fungal enzymes work faster and spores grow more quickly. IV: temperature; DV: days until mould is first visible (or area covered after 5 days).

items.stem: "School science should only use computer simulations to avoid laboratory hazards." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Simulations are useful, but managed hands-on practical work is essential for learning science.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no risk of burns, cuts or chemical injury; cheaper and no waste. Arguments against: students do not learn practical and safety skills; real experiments show real errors and surprises; hazards can be managed by risk assessment. Supported judgement: Simulations are useful, but managed hands-on practical work is essential for learning science. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Ana investigated how the mass hung on a spring affects the extension of the spring. The method had this weakness: the ruler was read from above. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: read the pointer at eye level to avoid parallax error
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: read the pointer at eye level to avoid parallax error

items.stem: "Results from a single, very careful experiment are enough to draw a firm conclusion." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: A single experiment gives limited evidence; repeats and reproduction by others are needed for a firm conclusion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: careful technique reduces errors. Arguments against: random errors and anomalies can only be detected by repeating; other scientists must reproduce results; a single sample may not be representative. Supported judgement: A single experiment gives limited evidence; repeats and reproduction by others are needed for a firm conclusion. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which type of graph is used when the independent variable is categoric (e.g. type of material)?
items.answer: Bar chart
items.markingKey: B. Categoric data have no numerical order.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A statement of what you expect to happen in an experiment, often in the form "if … then …""?
items.answer: prediction
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of prediction.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "resolution".
items.answer: The smallest change an instrument can measure, e.g. 1 mm on a ruler
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the smallest change an instrument can measure, e.g. 1 mm on a ruler. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a conclusion should quote data from the results.
items.answer: Quoting values provides evidence for the trend described, so the conclusion is supported rather than just stated.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Quoting values provides evidence for the trend described, so the conclusion is supported rather than just stated. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Human error means I made a mistake, so it should be in every evaluation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Evaluations should name the specific source of error (e.g. reaction time when using a stopwatch) and suggest a specific improvement.
items.markingKey: Evaluations should name the specific source of error (e.g. reaction time when using a stopwatch) and suggest a specific improvement. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "A fair test means doing the experiment only once so nothing changes." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A fair test changes only the independent variable; repeating trials improves reliability.
items.markingKey: A fair test changes only the independent variable; repeating trials improves reliability. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a theory and a hypothesis.
items.answer: A hypothesis is a testable prediction for a particular investigation; a theory is a broad explanation that has been tested many times and is supported by lots of evidence.
items.markingKey: A hypothesis is a testable prediction for a particular investigation; a theory is a broad explanation that has been tested many times and is supported by lots of evidence. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a risk and a hazard.
items.answer: A hazard is something that could cause harm (e.g. hot water); a risk is the chance of harm happening and how serious it would be.
items.markingKey: A hazard is something that could cause harm (e.g. hot water); a risk is the chance of harm happening and how serious it would be. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a bar chart and a line graph.
items.answer: A bar chart is used when the independent variable is categoric (types); a line graph is used when both variables are continuous numbers.
items.markingKey: A bar chart is used when the independent variable is categoric (types); a line graph is used when both variables are continuous numbers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Omar and three classmates each timed a ball rolling down the same ramp with stopwatches, three times each, while the ramp height was changed.

Ramp height / cm | Time / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 3.10 | 3.25 | 3.15
20 | 2.36 | 2.26 | 2.30
30 | 1.81 | 1.93 | 1.82
40 | 1.64 | 1.65 | 1.65
50 | 1.44 | 1.45 | 1.45

Calculate the mean time when the ramp height was 20 cm.
items.markingKey: M1 (2.36 + 2.26 + 2.30) ÷ 3; A1 2.31 s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Rafael is investigating how the type of insulation around a beaker affects how fast hot water cools. State the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables.
items.answer: IV: type of insulating material; DV: temperature drop in 10 minutes; controls: starting temperature, volume of water, thickness of insulation, room temperature
items.markingKey: 1 IV type of insulating material; 1 DV temperature drop in 10 minutes; 1-2 any two valid controls from: starting temperature, volume of water, thickness of insulation, room temperature.

items.stem:
Jonas timed how long a sugar cube took to dissolve in 100 cm³ of water at different temperatures, without stirring.

Temperature / °C | Time to dissolve / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
20 | 277 | 279 | 265
30 | 202 | 199 | 208
40 | 169 | 163 | 219
50 | 135 | 137 | 137
60 | 117 | 119 | 118

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean time to dissolve at 40 °C, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 219 s (trial 3 at 40 °C); mean = 166.0 s
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (219) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 166.0 s.

items.stem: Sana writes: "A beaker is the best apparatus for measuring 37 cm³ of water." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Beakers have rough scales; a 50 cm³ measuring cylinder (or burette) gives a much more accurate volume.
items.markingKey: Beakers have rough scales; a 50 cm³ measuring cylinder (or burette) gives a much more accurate volume. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student’s results: x = 1, 2, 3, 4; y = 2, 4, 6, 8. Show that y is directly proportional to x and predict y when x = 7.
items.answer: y/x = 2 for every pair (and the line passes through the origin); y = 14
items.markingKey: 1 ratio y/x constant = 2 (or doubling x doubles y); 1 straight line through origin; 1 y = 2 × 7 = 14.

items.stem: A balance reads 0.2 g when empty. A student records masses of 29.2, 26.0, 23.7 g without noticing. (a) Name this type of error. (b) Give the correct masses.
items.answer: (a) zero (systematic) error (b) 29.0, 25.8, 23.5 g
items.markingKey: (a) 1 zero/systematic error. (b) 1-2 subtract 0.2 g from each reading.

items.stem:
Yusuf measured the time for 10 swings of a pendulum of different lengths and calculated the period of one swing.

Length / cm | Period / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
20 | 0.80 | 0.79 | 0.84
40 | 1.16 | 1.15 | 1.58
60 | 1.41 | 1.45 | 1.45
80 | 1.64 | 1.66 | 1.69
100 | 1.78 | 1.90 | 1.83

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean period at 40 cm, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 1.58 s (trial 3 at 40 cm); mean = 1.15 s

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the temperature of water affects the time taken for a sugar cube to dissolve. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Heat water and measure 100 cm³ into a beaker at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C (check with a thermometer); drop in one sugar cube and start the stopwatch; do not stir; stop when no solid remains; repeat three times at each temperature; calculate means and plot a line graph.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (hot water can scald – use a heat-proof mat and handle beakers with tongs). Model: Heat water and measure 100 cm³ into a beaker at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C (check with a thermometer); drop in one sugar cube and start the stopwatch; do not stir; stop when no solid remains; repeat three times at each temperature; calculate means and plot a line graph.

items.stem: Omar plans an investigation into how the mass hung on a spring affects the extension of the spring. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (mass hung on the spring (100 g to 600 g in 100 g steps)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.
